\chapter{A Tree}
\label{ch:ta-a-tree}
\hlchaptermodality{52}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a tree, its branch, its new shoot, its root and its seed in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C52-seed and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[maram]{\ta{மரம்} (maram) — a tree}

\label{lesson:TA-C52-tree}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{viṇmīṉ} mean, and what did \emph{mēkam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மரம்}}
\textbf{\ta{மரம்}} (\emph{maram}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*mar-}, and Malayalam did not lay a finger on it: \ml{മരം}, the same word letter for letter. Telugu went somewhere else entirely, to \te{చెట్టు} (\emph{ceṭṭu}) — the ordinary arrangement in this family, where the two closest sisters agree and the third has its own.

\emph{maram} is the tree standing and the timber cut out of it. A carpenter works in \emph{maram}; so does a forest.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five pieces of one tree.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maram}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mēkam}, then \emph{maram}, the cloud and what stands under it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மரம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tree\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kiḷai]{\ta{கிளை} (kiḷai) — a branch}

\label{lesson:TA-C52-branch}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maram} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கிளை}}
\textbf{\ta{கிளை}} (\emph{kiḷai}) — \textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.

Both sisters reach for a word of a different shape here — Malayalam \emph{kompŭ}, Telugu \emph{komma} — where Tamil says \ta{கிளை}.

And a \ta{கிளை} is not only what grows off a tree. A family has them: the branch of a house, the people who come off one trunk. When Tamil calls somebody your \emph{kiḷai}, it is the tree word doing the work, and a bank branch is a \emph{kiḷai} too.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the trunk, and what comes off it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kiḷai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maram}, then \emph{kiḷai}, the tree and then what comes off it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{கிளை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a branch\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[taḷir]{\ta{தளிர்} (taḷir) — a tender shoot}

\label{lesson:TA-C52-shoot}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kiḷai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{தளிர்}}
\textbf{\ta{தளிர்}} (\emph{taḷir}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tender shoot\textquotedblright{}.

The new growth at the end of a branch: the pale soft leaf before it hardens and goes green. Tamil keeps a word of its own for it rather than calling it a small leaf, which tells you how much attention the thing has had.

\emph{taḷirkka} is what a tree does after the first rains. Tamil says it of people as well — somebody who has been ill and is picking up again has \emph{taḷirttu}, put out new growth.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: the tree, the branch, and the newest thing on it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{taḷir}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kiḷai}, then \emph{taḷir}, the branch and the new thing on the end of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{தளிர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tender shoot\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vēr]{\ta{வேர்} (vēr) — a root}

\label{lesson:TA-C52-root}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{taḷir} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வேர்}}
\textbf{\ta{வேர்}} (\emph{vēr}) — \textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.

One word in three hands. Malayalam \ml{വേര്} (\emph{vērŭ}), Telugu \te{వేరు} (\emph{vēru}), Tamil \ta{வேர்}. Set them beside each other and there is nothing left to choose between them.

It is the root of a plant and the bottom of anything else: a tooth has a \ta{வேர்}, and so does a word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four: everything above ground, and now the part under it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vēr}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{taḷir}, then \emph{vēr}, the top of the tree and the bottom of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வேர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a root\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vitai]{\ta{விதை} (vitai) — a seed}

\label{lesson:TA-C52-seed}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vēr} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{விதை}}
\textbf{\ta{விதை}} (\emph{vitai}) — \textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.

Malayalam \ml{വിത്ത്} (\emph{vittŭ}) and Telugu \te{విత్తనం} (\emph{vittanaṁ}) are the same root wearing different endings, and Tamil keeps a \emph{vittu} of its own beside \ta{விதை}.

\ta{விதை} is the seed and the sowing of it at once: \emph{vitaikka} is to sow. The thing and what you do with it share one shape, which saves Tamil a word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A whole tree, from the seed under it to the softest thing on the end of a branch.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vitai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{maram}, \emph{kiḷai}, \emph{taḷir}, \emph{vēr}, \emph{vitai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{விதை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
